y-m-04-01.title: The same number 245: can the models be different?
y-m-04-01.topic: Place value of three-digit numbers (showing with hundreds, tens, and ones models)
y-m-04-01.goal: Check that the same three-digit number can be shown in several ways by changing the combination of models, and explain why the whole number is the same even when the number of models is different.
y-m-04-01.material: Play with number models. A hundreds model shows 100, a tens model shows 10, and a ones model shows 1. There are plenty of each kind of model. Minho showed 245 with 2 hundreds models, 4 tens models, and 5 ones models. Seoa said, 'This is the only way to show 245.'
y-m-04-01.thinking.1: Making several solutions within the conditions
y-m-04-01.thinking.2: Comparing different ways of showing the same value
y-m-04-01.prereq.0: Reading and writing a three-digit number by splitting it into the hundreds, tens, and ones places (Grade 2 level)
y-m-04-01.s.s1.prompt: What do you think of Seoa's words? Can you show 245 with fewer than 2 hundreds models?
y-m-04-01.s.s1.hint.0: Write how much the whole goes down when you take away one hundreds model.
y-m-04-01.s.s1.hint.1: Count how many tens models you would need to put down to fill in the amount that went down.
y-m-04-01.s.s1.o.a: No. The hundreds digit of 245 is 2, so there must be exactly 2 hundreds models
y-m-04-01.s.s1.r.a: This idea matched the digit 2 straight to 2 hundreds models. When showing with models, also think about whether 100 can be shown with other models.
y-m-04-01.s.s1.o.b: Yes. You can show the 100 that a hundreds model shows with other models
y-m-04-01.s.s1.r.b: This idea saw that the value of one model can be shown with several other models. Check which models and how many to use.
y-m-04-01.s.s1.o.c: You can't tell. Because you don't know how many models there are
y-m-04-01.s.s1.r.c: This idea missed a condition. It is already written that there are plenty of models. Read the condition again and then judge.
y-m-04-01.s.s1.explain: If you take away 1 hundreds model (100) and put down 10 tens models (100), the whole stays 245. There is a way to use only 1 hundreds model, so the words 'the only one' are not right.
y-m-04-01.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different ways to show 245. Show it with a hundreds models, b tens models, and c ones models. Use at most 9 ones models (we agreed that when there would be 10 ones models, we swap them for 1 tens model).
y-m-04-01.s.s2.hint.0: First think about how many ones models there must be for the ones place to be right.
y-m-04-01.s.s2.hint.1: Reduce the hundreds models one at a time and fill the amount that went down with tens models.
y-m-04-01.s.s2.ok.c1: The number of models is 0 or more.
y-m-04-01.s.s2.fail.c1: The number of models must be 0 or more.
y-m-04-01.s.s2.ok.c2: You used whole models without cutting them.
y-m-04-01.s.s2.fail.c2: Models cannot be cut, so the number must be a number you can count, like 0, 1, 2....
y-m-04-01.s.s2.fail.c3: The numbers shown by the hundreds models, tens models, and ones models must add up to 245.
y-m-04-01.s.s2.ok.c4: There are 9 or fewer ones models.
y-m-04-01.s.s2.fail.c4: We agreed to use at most 9 ones models.
y-m-04-01.s.s2.explain: If there are 9 or fewer ones models, the ones models are fixed at 5, and only the way of splitting the other 240 between hundreds models and tens models changes. (2, 4, 5), (1, 14, 5), and (0, 24, 5) are all possible.
y-m-04-01.s.s2.because.prompt: Write why the whole is exactly 245 even when the numbers of models are different.
y-m-04-01.s.s2.because.hint.0: Choose one of the combinations you made and say which model you swapped for which models.
y-m-04-01.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write how many tens models are the same as the number shown by one hundreds model.
y-m-04-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: In your explanation, is the number of models you swap for one hundreds model clear?
y-m-04-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Does it include the words that the whole number stays the same even when you swap the models?
y-m-04-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you use one of the combinations you made as an example?
y-m-04-01.s.s2.because.model.0: 1 hundreds model is the same as 10 tens models, so the whole stays the same even if you swap them. So even if you change (2, 4, 5) to (1, 14, 5), it is 245.
y-m-04-01.s.s2.because.model.1: If you take away one hundreds model, 100 goes down, but if you put down 10 more tens models, 100 goes up, so the sum is the same.
y-m-04-01.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: An explanation that spells out the swapping as 'take away and add'.
y-m-04-01.s.s3.prompt: Among the ways you just made, which one uses the fewest models? Count the number of models by adding the hundreds models, tens models, and ones models all together.
y-m-04-01.s.s3.hint.0: Choose the three ways one at a time and write the total number of models.
y-m-04-01.s.s3.hint.1: Put the totals side by side and find the smallest.
y-m-04-01.s.s3.o.a: 0 hundreds models, 24 tens models, 5 ones models
y-m-04-01.s.s3.r.a: If you do not use hundreds models at all, the tens models become the most. When the kinds of models decrease, the number can actually increase.
y-m-04-01.s.s3.o.b: 1 hundreds model, 14 tens models, 5 ones models
y-m-04-01.s.s3.r.b: If you reduce the hundreds models, you need that many more tens models. Add up the numbers of all three ways and compare.
y-m-04-01.s.s3.o.c: 2 hundreds models, 4 tens models, 5 ones models
y-m-04-01.s.s3.r.c: This idea added up and compared the number of models in each of the three ways.
y-m-04-01.s.s3.explain: The numbers of models are 29, 20, and 11. The more models of large value you use, the fewer the number of models. Even for the same number, the number of models differs depending on which models you use.

y-m-04-02.title: 4 on each of 3 plates, 3 on each of 4 plates
y-m-04-02.topic: Meaning of multiplication (the number in one bundle and the number of bundles)
y-m-04-02.goal: Check with an array of dots why 3×4 and 4×3 have the same value, and tell apart that even when the values are the same, the 'story' (the number of bundles and the number in one bundle) is not the same.
y-m-04-02.material: Read the multiplication 3×4 to mean '4 bundles of 3', and 4×3 to mean '3 bundles of 4'. (3×4 is read "three times four" and 4×3 is read "four times three".) Each plate has the same number of apples, and no apples are left over or missing. Doyun said, 'Four plates of 3 and three plates of 4 are bundled differently, so the number of apples will be different too.'
y-m-04-02.thinking.0: Holding off on judging before checking
y-m-04-02.thinking.1: Fixing your judgment and how sure you are with new information
y-m-04-02.thinking.2: Telling apart what is the same and what is different
y-m-04-02.prereq.0: Counting by bundles of the same number (Grade 2 level)
y-m-04-02.prereq.1: Part of the 3 and 4 times tables
y-m-04-02.s.s1.prompt: Think through Doyun's words by looking at information step by step.
y-m-04-02.s.s1.hint.0: To check Doyun's words, count the apples yourself or draw them as dots.
y-m-04-02.s.s1.hint.1: Look at how the rows change when you view the same dots from another direction.
y-m-04-02.s.s1.st.0.info: Doyun has not counted the apples yet. For '4 plates of 3' and '3 plates of 4', the number of plates and the number of apples on one plate are different from each other.
y-m-04-02.s.s1.st.0.ask: How do you see Doyun's words now?
y-m-04-02.s.s1.st.0.after: Nothing has been counted yet, so it is hard to say they are right or wrong. So let's draw them as dots.
y-m-04-02.s.s1.st.0.o.a: That's right. If the way of bundling is different, the total number is different too
y-m-04-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This idea straight away believed that if the way of bundling is different, the total is different too.
y-m-04-02.s.s1.st.0.o.b: You can't tell yet. You have to count or draw to check
y-m-04-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This idea held off on judging because there is no evidence.
y-m-04-02.s.s1.st.0.o.c: That's wrong. Even if the bundles are different, the total number is always the same
y-m-04-02.s.s1.st.0.r.c: The conclusion may be right, but this idea asserted it without checking.
y-m-04-02.s.s1.st.1.info: 12 dots were placed in three rows with 4 across. When the paper was turned sideways without adding or removing a single dot, it became four rows with 3 across.
y-m-04-02.s.s1.st.1.ask: Looking at this information, how did your thinking about Doyun's words change?
y-m-04-02.s.s1.st.1.after: Both the idea of checking with one example and then testing more, and the idea that the reason 'the dots stay the same when turned' works for other numbers too, are reasonable.
y-m-04-02.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The number of apples still looks different
y-m-04-02.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This idea felt that the number changed even though the dots were turned. Check whether you ever added or removed a dot.
y-m-04-02.s.s1.st.1.o.b: In this case they are the same. I want to check more whether it is so for other numbers too
y-m-04-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This idea confirms sameness in one example and wants to look at other cases separately.
y-m-04-02.s.s1.st.1.o.c: You can just turn the dots, so you can say the number is the same in multiplication of other numbers too
y-m-04-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This idea saw that the reason 'the number of dots does not change when turned' works for other numbers too.
y-m-04-02.s.s1.st.2.info: The apples in the two cases are the same, 12. Doyun said again, 'The number of apples is the same, so the two stories are exactly the same.'
y-m-04-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: What is the same and what is different?
y-m-04-02.s.s1.st.2.after: The number of apples is the same, 12, but 3 plates and 4 plates, and 4 on a plate and 3 on a plate, are different. Even if the values are the same, the stories are not the same.
y-m-04-02.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Both the number of apples and the number of plates are exactly the same
y-m-04-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This idea widely thought that because the number of apples is the same, everything is the same. Compare the first number of plates.
y-m-04-02.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Both the number of apples and the number of plates are different
y-m-04-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This idea went back to the first expectation. We checked with the dot array whether the number of apples is the same.
y-m-04-02.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The number of apples is the same and the number of plates is different
y-m-04-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This idea separated what is the same and what is different.
y-m-04-02.s.s1.reflect: At first, you could hold off on judging because you had not checked yet. When you turned the dots, you got the evidence that 'the number is the same', and when you came back to the plate story, how far you can say 'the same' (only the number is the same) changed. Say what information changed what judgment.
y-m-04-02.s.s2.prompt: Mina explained the two multiplications. Pick the line where the story does not fit.
y-m-04-02.s.s2.hint.0: Separate whether each line is about the 'value' or about the 'story'.
y-m-04-02.s.s2.hint.1: Find whether anything differs between the case of 4 on each of 3 plates and the case of 3 on each of 4 plates.
y-m-04-02.s.s2.line.0: 4×3 is 3 bundles of 4, so it is 4, 8, 12, which makes 12.
y-m-04-02.s.s2.line.1: 3×4 is 4 bundles of 3, so it is 3, 6, 9, 12, which makes 12.
y-m-04-02.s.s2.line.2: The values are the same, so 4×3 and 3×4 have exactly the same story too.
y-m-04-02.s.s2.line.3: So the number of apples is the same when you put 4 on each of 3 plates and when you put 3 on each of 4 plates.
y-m-04-02.s.s2.explain: Line 3 is wrong. Even if the values are the same, the number of plates and the number of apples on one plate are different from each other, so the stories are not the same. Lines 1, 2, and 4 are right.
y-m-04-02.s.s3.prompt: Tell Doyun in one or two sentences. Write it including both what is the same and what is different in the two cases.
y-m-04-02.s.s3.hint.0: First write how many apples there are in all, then compare the number of plates and the number of apples on one plate.
y-m-04-02.s.s3.hint.1: Write separately what 'the same' and 'different' are each about.
y-m-04-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say clearly, with numbers or words, what is the same?
y-m-04-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say what is different by mentioning plates or bundles?
y-m-04-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you avoid saying Doyun's words are simply right or simply wrong?
y-m-04-02.s.s3.model.0: In both cases there are 12 apples, the same. But whether there are 3 plates or 4 plates, and how many on one plate, are different.
y-m-04-02.s.s3.model.1: The total number of apples is the same, but 3 on each of 4 plates and 4 on each of 3 plates are different stories.
y-m-04-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: Said what is different all at once with the words 'the stories are different'.

y-m-04-03.title: Can we trust Seojun's check?
y-m-04-03.topic: Odd and even numbers (finding a counterexample and a reason by pairing marbles)
y-m-04-03.goal: Understand that for a claim to be confirmed by a few calculations, the examples must test the cases the claim is about, make a counterexample, and explain the reason by pairing.
y-m-04-03.material: When you pair marbles two by two, if none is left over it is even, and if one is left over it is odd. (4 and 6 are even, 5 and 7 are odd.) Only think about the numbers 1 to 30. Seojun tried a few calculations and said, 'If you add two odd numbers, you get an odd number.'
y-m-04-03.thinking.0: Think about whether the cases checked are the same as the cases the claim talks about
y-m-04-03.thinking.2: Tell apart which of the number of examples and the reason supports the claim
y-m-04-03.prereq.1: Telling even and odd apart by pairing two by two (Grade 2 level; the meaning is given in the material)
y-m-04-03.s.s1.line.3: An odd number came out all three times, so adding two odd numbers gives an odd number.
y-m-04-03.s.s2.prompt: Make examples that do not fit Seojun's words. Choose different odd numbers a and b (from 1 to 30), test whether Seojun's words are right, and make 3 examples that do not fit Seojun's words. Writing a and b swapped is the same example.
y-m-04-03.s.s2.hint.0: First write whether the sum must be odd or even for Seojun's words to be right.
y-m-04-03.s.s2.hint.1: Add two small odd numbers and pair the sum with marbles.
y-m-04-03.s.s2.ok.c2: They are different numbers from 1 to 30.
y-m-04-03.s.s2.fail.c2: They must be two different numbers from 1 to 30.
y-m-04-03.s.s2.ok.c3: The sum is not odd. It does not fit Seojun's words.
y-m-04-03.s.s2.fail.c3: The sum became odd. It is not an example that does not fit Seojun's words.
y-m-04-03.s.s2.explain: When odd numbers are added to each other, the sum is always even, so whichever two odd numbers you pick, they do not fit Seojun's words. For example, 3 and 5 have a sum of 8.
y-m-04-03.s.s2.because.prompt: Explain with marble pairing why the sum of two odd numbers is even every time.
y-m-04-03.s.s2.because.hint.0: Put out two odd numbers of marbles and pair them two by two. Are there leftover marbles?
y-m-04-03.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write what to do with the leftover marbles.
y-m-04-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Does it include that an odd number of marbles has something left over when paired?
y-m-04-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you write what happens to the leftovers too?
y-m-04-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you explain by using one example you made?
y-m-04-03.s.s2.because.model.0: With an odd number of marbles, pairing two by two leaves one. With two odd numbers, the two leftovers become a pair too, so everything is paired up, and it is even.
y-m-04-03.s.s2.because.model.1: If you put out 3 and 5 as marbles and pair them, one is left from each, and those two become a pair, so the sum is even. Other odd numbers are the same.
y-m-04-03.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: Gave one example and went on to 'other odd numbers are the same'.
y-m-04-03.s.s3.prompt: With the 3 examples you just made, can you say 'adding two odd numbers is always even'?
y-m-04-03.s.s3.hint.0: Find whether there is anything in your pairing explanation that applies only to 3 and 5.
y-m-04-03.s.s3.hint.1: Say in words whether the same explanation works for other pairs of odd numbers, like 7 and 11, or 15 and 21.
y-m-04-03.s.s3.explain: The pairing explanation (when paired two by two, one is left each time, and the two leftovers become a pair) works as it is for any odd number. So you can say it after having the reason too. Looking for more examples is also a reasonable attitude of holding off on asserting.
y-m-04-03.s.s3.acc.0: Looking for more examples and holding off on asserting is also reasonable. Checking the reason too makes it more certain.

y-m-04-04.title: What pattern do the numbers in the colored boxes have?
y-m-04-04.topic: Finding patterns in a number chart
y-m-04-04.goal: Sort out the patterns that can be stated in several ways from the same colored boxes, learn that a pattern depends on the shape of the chart (the number of boxes in a row), and find the pattern again in a new chart.
y-m-04-04.material:
This is a number chart with 5 numbers in each row, written from 1 to 25. The third box in each row is colored. The colored numbers are 3, 8, 13, 18, and 23.
Row 1: 1 2 3 4 5
Row 2: 6 7 8 9 10
Row 3: 11 12 13 14 15
Row 4: 16 17 18 19 20
Row 5: 21 22 23 24 25
y-m-04-04.thinking.0: Sorting out which of several explanations of the pattern are right
y-m-04-04.thinking.1: Finding the condition under which a pattern holds
y-m-04-04.thinking.2: Making the pattern again in a new chart
y-m-04-04.prereq.0: Knowing the order of numbers up to 100
y-m-04-04.prereq.1: Reading an arrangement where numbers grow by a constant amount (Grade 2 level)
y-m-04-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the statements that are right about the colored numbers.
y-m-04-04.s.s1.hint.0: Write the colored numbers in row order and look at how different two neighboring numbers are.
y-m-04-04.s.s1.hint.1: Write down only the ones digit of each number.
y-m-04-04.s.s1.o.a: All the colored numbers are odd
y-m-04-04.s.s1.r.a: This idea was said by looking at only a part without checking 3, 8, 13... one by one. 8 and 18 are even.
y-m-04-04.s.s1.o.b: The ones digit of the colored numbers repeats as 3, 8, 3, 8...
y-m-04-04.s.s1.r.b: This idea found the pattern where the ones digit repeats.
y-m-04-04.s.s1.o.c: The colored numbers start from 3 and grow by 5
y-m-04-04.s.s1.r.c: This idea looked at the difference between neighboring colored numbers.
y-m-04-04.s.s1.o.d: All the colored numbers have a ones digit of 3 or 8
y-m-04-04.s.s1.r.d: This idea gathered the ones digits of the numbers and looked at them.
y-m-04-04.s.s1.explain: 3, 8, 13, 18, and 23 grow by 5, and the ones digit alternates between 3 and 8. 8 and 18 are even, so 'all odd' is not right. The same row of numbers can be described in several ways.
y-m-04-04.s.s2.prompt: We made a new chart by writing the same numbers with 6 in each row. This time too the third box of each row was colored, and the colored numbers became 3, 9, 15, and 21. Hyeonseo said, 'The pattern of growing by 5 is a property of the numbers themselves, so it's right in any chart.' What do you think?
y-m-04-04.s.s2.hint.0: Look at how different neighboring colored numbers are in the new chart.
y-m-04-04.s.s2.hint.1: Compare that value with the number of boxes in a row.
y-m-04-04.s.s2.o.a: Hyeonseo is right. The numbers are the same, so the pattern is the same in any chart
y-m-04-04.s.s2.r.a: This idea saw that if the numbers are the same, the colored boxes are the same too. First check the colored numbers in the new chart.
y-m-04-04.s.s2.o.b: If you change the chart, the colored numbers have no pattern at all
y-m-04-04.s.s2.r.b: This idea saw the pattern changing as the pattern disappearing. Look again at 3, 9, 15, 21.
y-m-04-04.s.s2.o.c: The pattern of growing by 5 is right only in the chart with 5 in each row
y-m-04-04.s.s2.r.c: This idea saw that the pattern depends on the shape of the chart.
y-m-04-04.s.s2.explain: When a row has 5 boxes, going to the box below grows by 5, and when it has 6, it grows by 6. The pattern depends on the shape of the chart, not only on the numbers.
y-m-04-04.s.s3.prompt: In the chart with 6 in each row, write at least 4 colored numbers that continue right below 3, including the ones that came up earlier, and write in one sentence what the pattern is.
y-m-04-04.s.s3.hint.0: Count the number in the third box of the second row of the new chart.
y-m-04-04.s.s3.hint.1: Look at how different neighboring colored numbers are and write it as a pattern.
y-m-04-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check that the differences between the numbers you wrote are all the same?
y-m-04-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Does the number in your pattern connect to the number of boxes in a row?
y-m-04-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you guess the next colored number using the pattern?
y-m-04-04.s.s3.model.0: It is 3, 9, 15, 21. The pattern is that it grows by 6.
y-m-04-04.s.s3.model.1: 3 to 9 to 15 to 21. A row has 6 boxes, so each time you go down you add 6.
y-m-04-04.s.s3.modelNote.1: Wrote it connecting the number of boxes in a row with the pattern.

y-m-04-05.title: What color is the 20th bead?
y-m-04-05.topic: Predicting the order in a repeating pattern
y-m-04-05.goal: Find the 20th of a repeating pattern by drawing, skip counting, looking at bundles, and so on, find and fix the wrong line, and explain again in words a younger sibling can understand.
y-m-04-05.material: You are making a bead necklace. Take 1 red bead and 2 blue beads as one round and keep stringing them in the same order. The 1st bead is red, the 2nd and 3rd are blue, and the 4th is red again. Haeun wants to know the color of the 20th bead. There are far more than 20 beads strung.
y-m-04-05.thinking.1: Finding the wrong place in an explanation
y-m-04-05.thinking.2: Rewriting an explanation to suit the listener
y-m-04-05.prereq.0: Saying the rule of a repeating pattern (Grade 2 level)
y-m-04-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the suitable methods for finding the color of the 20th bead.
y-m-04-05.s.s1.hint.0: Write the colors from the 1st to the 4th and check at which number red comes up again.
y-m-04-05.s.s1.hint.1: Write separately only the numbers where red comes up and look at what pattern they have.
y-m-04-05.s.s1.o.a: The 3rd, 6th, 9th... are red, so look at the multiples of 3 near 20
y-m-04-05.s.s1.r.a: This idea misread the numbers where red comes up. Check again the colors of the 1st and 4th beads.
y-m-04-05.s.s1.o.b: Draw the beads in order from the 1st to the 20th
y-m-04-05.s.s1.r.b: This is a method that tries to check by laying them out directly one at a time.
y-m-04-05.s.s1.o.c: Skip count by 3s the numbers where red comes up, 1, 4, 7..., and go close to 20
y-m-04-05.s.s1.r.c: This is a method that saw that the numbers of the red beads form a pattern.
y-m-04-05.s.s1.o.d: Look at only the first 5 and decide the rest by feeling
y-m-04-05.s.s1.r.d: This is a method that decides by guessing without using the pattern. There is no evidence you can check.
y-m-04-05.s.s1.explain: Both the method of drawing and the method of skip counting the red numbers find the 20th. The statement that the multiples of 3 are red is not right. The 3rd is blue.
y-m-04-05.s.s2.line.0: The red beads are the 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th beads.
y-m-04-05.s.s2.line.1: Between one red bead and the next red bead there are 2 blue beads.
y-m-04-05.s.s2.line.2: The next red beads are the 13th, 16th, and 20th beads.
y-m-04-05.s.s2.line.3: The 20th is a red bead, so the 20th bead is red.
y-m-04-05.s.s3.prompt: Explain in easy words to a Grade 1 younger sibling how to find the color of the 20th bead. Write it with numbers in it.
y-m-04-05.s.s3.hint.0: First write a few numbers where red beads come up.
y-m-04-05.s.s3.hint.1: Instead of words the younger sibling doesn't know, say things like 'let's draw it' and 'let's count it'.
y-m-04-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write it in an order the younger sibling can follow?
y-m-04-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you use numbers or picture talk instead of hard words?
y-m-04-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you say all the way what color the 20th is?
y-m-04-05.s.s3.model.0: Draw them cutting every 3, with red, blue, blue as one bundle. Red is at the 1st, 4th, 7th.... If you count skipping by 3s, the 19th is red and the 20th is blue.
y-m-04-05.s.s3.model.1: Let's draw the beads in order up to the 20th. If you keep drawing red, blue, blue, the 20th becomes blue.
y-m-04-05.s.s3.modelNote.1: An explanation that focuses on the one method of drawing.

y-m-04-06.title: How many matchsticks are needed?
y-m-04-06.topic: Pattern of how the number grows in an arrangement of shapes
y-m-04-06.goal: Count to check which of two patterns fits the real data, explain why the pattern is right by sharing sides, and use the pattern to predict the value for a bigger case.
y-m-04-06.material: You make squares joined in one row with matchsticks. A square attached on the side shares one side with the previous square. One square is made with 4 matchsticks. Minjae said, 'Each time the squares go up by one, the matchsticks go up by 4.' Gaon said, 'The first square takes 4, and from then on each time it goes up by one, it goes up by 3.'
y-m-04-06.thinking.0: Evaluating two patterns by comparing them with the data
y-m-04-06.thinking.1: Fixing your judgment with new information
y-m-04-06.thinking.2: Explaining the reason for a pattern
y-m-04-06.prereq.0: Knowing the sides of a square (Grade 2 level)
y-m-04-06.s.s1.prompt: If you join 2 squares so that they share one side, how many matchsticks are needed in all?
y-m-04-06.s.s1.hint.0: First write the number needed when the 2 squares are placed separately.
y-m-04-06.s.s1.hint.1: Count how many sides the two squares share.
y-m-04-06.s.s1.r.a: This idea subtracted the shared side twice when counting. The two squares share one side.
y-m-04-06.s.s1.r.b: This idea counted the shared side only once.
y-m-04-06.s.s1.r.c: This idea counted 4 for each square separately. Check again whether there is a shared side.
y-m-04-06.s.s1.explain: If you make 2 squares separately it is 8, but they share one side, so one overlaps and it is 7.
y-m-04-06.s.s2.prompt: When you joined 3 squares and counted, there were 10 matchsticks. Which of the two matches the results counted so far (4 for 1, 7 for 2, 10 for 3)?
y-m-04-06.s.s2.hint.0: Calculate and write the numbers for 2 and 3 squares following Minjae's words.
y-m-04-06.s.s2.hint.1: Calculate following Gaon's words too and put it side by side with the counted results.
y-m-04-06.s.s2.o.a: Only Minjae's words match the results counted so far
y-m-04-06.s.s2.r.a: Calculate how many it is for 2 squares following Minjae's words and compare with the counted result.
y-m-04-06.s.s2.o.b: Both people's words match the results counted so far
y-m-04-06.s.s2.r.b: This idea did not check each of the two statements against the directly counted results.
y-m-04-06.s.s2.o.c: Only Gaon's words match the results counted so far
y-m-04-06.s.s2.r.c: This idea compared the two patterns against the data.
y-m-04-06.s.s2.o.d: Neither person's words match the results counted so far
y-m-04-06.s.s2.r.d: Check again whether one of the two patterns matches the counted results.
y-m-04-06.s.s2.explain: By Minjae's words it should be 4, 8, 12, but the counted results are 4, 7, 10. Gaon's words match 4, 7, 10. But we checked only up to 3, so for bigger cases we need to check the reason.
y-m-04-06.s.s3.prompt: Using Gaon's pattern, predict the number of matchsticks needed when you join squares from 4 to 15. Make 3 pairs of the number of squares n and the number of matchsticks s.
y-m-04-06.s.s3.hint.0: Continue writing the numbers after the counted results 4, 7, 10 following the pattern.
y-m-04-06.s.s3.hint.1: Decide the case of 4 first, and for the rest add 3 each time the squares go up by one.
y-m-04-06.s.s3.ok.c1: The number of squares is from 4 to 15.
y-m-04-06.s.s3.fail.c1: The number of squares must be from 4 to 15.
y-m-04-06.s.s3.ok.c2: It matches Gaon's pattern (starting from 4 and growing by 3).
y-m-04-06.s.s3.fail.c2: It does not match Gaon's pattern (4 at first, then 3 each time it goes up by one).
y-m-04-06.s.s3.explain: It grows by 3 each time: 13 when there are 4 squares, 16 when there are 5. With 7 squares it is 22, and with 10 squares it is 31.
y-m-04-06.s.s3.because.prompt: Write why only 3 matchsticks are needed when you attach one more square.
y-m-04-06.s.s3.because.hint.0: Separate the sides you have to newly put down and the sides that are already there when you attach a square.
y-m-04-06.s.s3.because.hint.1: Using the difference between 2 squares and 3 squares, say in words what overlaps.
y-m-04-06.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: Did you say how many of the 4 sides of the attached square are newly needed?
y-m-04-06.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: Did you talk about the side that overlaps with the previous square?
y-m-04-06.s.s3.because.selfAssess.2: Did you use one of the pairs you made as an example?
y-m-04-06.s.s3.because.model.0: The new square shares one side with the square next to it, so only 3 out of 4 more are needed.
y-m-04-06.s.s3.because.model.1: Each time you attach one, one middle side overlaps, so it grows by only 3, not 4.
y-m-04-06.s.s3.because.modelNote.1: Expressed the overlapping side as 'the middle side'.

y-m-04-07.title: What day of the week is the 3rd of next month?
y-m-04-07.topic: The pattern of dates on the same day of the week on a calendar
y-m-04-07.goal: Use the pattern that dates on the same day of the week on a calendar grow by a constant amount, and sort out what more information is needed to know the day of the week next month, and find it.
y-m-04-07.material: On the calendar of a certain month, the 3rd is a Tuesday. All you know is that this month has at least 28 days. (You do not yet know exactly how many days it has.) Only think about the dates of this month.
y-m-04-07.thinking.0: Finding a pattern that grows by a constant amount
y-m-04-07.thinking.1: Sorting out needed information and unneeded information
y-m-04-07.thinking.2: Finding it with the pattern when information is given
y-m-04-07.prereq.0: How to read a calendar (days of the week and dates, Grade 2 level)
y-m-04-07.prereq.1: The order of the days of the week in a week
y-m-04-07.s.s1.prompt: Write 3 or more dates that are Tuesdays in this month. You only know there are 28 days, so look only within dates up to the 28th.
y-m-04-07.s.s1.hint.0: Think of a calendar and how many days after the 3rd it becomes Tuesday again.
y-m-04-07.s.s1.hint.1: Repeat the same thing from the day you found.
y-m-04-07.s.s1.ok.c1: They are dates from the 1st to the 28th.
y-m-04-07.s.s1.fail.c1: The dates you know are the 1st to the 28th. Find them within that.
y-m-04-07.s.s1.ok.c2: It is a day that is the same day of the week as the 3rd.
y-m-04-07.s.s1.fail.c2: It is not a day that is the same day of the week as the 3rd.
y-m-04-07.s.s1.explain: The 10th, 7 days after the 3rd, the 17th, 7 days after that, and the 24th, 7 days after that, are all Tuesdays. If you know only up to the 28th, the 3rd, 10th, 17th, and 24th are Tuesdays.
y-m-04-07.s.s2.prompt: You want to know what day of the week the 3rd of next month is. Choose all the information below that lets you find it if you know it.
y-m-04-07.s.s2.hint.0: Think about what you need to know to go from the 3rd of this month to the 3rd of next month.
y-m-04-07.s.s2.hint.1: Check one by one whether each piece of information connects that path.
y-m-04-07.s.s2.o.a: How many days this month has
y-m-04-07.s.s2.r.a: This idea saw that if you know how many days this month has, you can connect the day of the week of the last day of this month and the day of the week of the 1st of next month and find it.
y-m-04-07.s.s2.o.b: How many days next month has
y-m-04-07.s.s2.r.b: This idea missed that the last day of next month is not used to decide the day of the week of the 3rd of next month.
y-m-04-07.s.s2.r.c: The name of the year does not change the already given '3rd is Tuesday'. Look at whether the information that the 3rd is a Tuesday is enough.
y-m-04-07.s.s2.o.d: What day of the week the 1st of next month is
y-m-04-07.s.s2.r.d: This idea saw that if you know the day of the week of the 1st of next month, you can use the fact that the 3rd is two days later.
y-m-04-07.s.s2.explain: If you know how many days this month has, you can know how many days it is from the 3rd of this month to the 3rd of next month. Even if you know the day of the week of the 1st of next month, you can know the day of the week of the 3rd, two days later. You do not need the number of days of next month or the name of the year.
y-m-04-07.s.s3.prompt: You were told this month has 31 days. What day of the week is the 3rd of next month?
y-m-04-07.s.s3.hint.0: First find what day of the week the last day (the 31st) of this month is.
y-m-04-07.s.s3.hint.1: The day after the last day is the 1st of next month. Count from there to the 3rd.
y-m-04-07.s.s3.r.a: This idea saw it as the same day of the week as the 3rd of this month. Count how many days it is from the 3rd of this month to the 3rd of next month.
y-m-04-07.s.s3.r.b: This idea mistook the day of the week of the 1st of next month for the day of the week of the 3rd.
y-m-04-07.s.s3.r.c: This idea comes from counting one day too few. Check once more the day of the week of the last day of this month.
y-m-04-07.s.s3.r.d: This idea counted from the day of the week of the last day of this month to the 3rd of next month.
y-m-04-07.s.s3.explain: If the 3rd is a Tuesday, the 10th, 17th, 24th, and 31st are Tuesdays. The 1st of next month is a Wednesday, the 2nd is a Thursday, and the 3rd is a Friday.

y-m-04-08.title: 15 wheels: which vehicles, and how many?
y-m-04-08.topic: Pattern of numbers when two kinds are mixed (number of wheels)
y-m-04-08.goal: When vehicles with 2 wheels and vehicles with 3 wheels are mixed, find in several ways within the conditions the cases where the number of wheels is 15, and check that a new condition narrows them down to one.
y-m-04-08.material: There are bicycles and tricycles in a parking lot. A bicycle has 2 wheels and a tricycle has 3 wheels. There is at least 1 of each kind, and there are 15 wheels in all. You do not yet know how many bicycles and how many tricycles there are. There are no other wheels.
y-m-04-08.thinking.0: Judging the possibility when there is only one kind
y-m-04-08.thinking.1: Making several solutions within the conditions
y-m-04-08.thinking.2: Narrowing the possible cases with a new condition
y-m-04-08.prereq.0: Counting by bundles of several (Grade 2 level)
y-m-04-08.s.s1.prompt: If there are only bicycles, could there be 15 wheels?
y-m-04-08.s.s1.hint.0: Write the number of wheels when there are 1, 2, 3... bicycles.
y-m-04-08.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether 15 is among the numbers you wrote.
y-m-04-08.s.s1.o.a: No. Skip counting by 2s gives 14, 16, so 15 does not come up
y-m-04-08.s.s1.r.a: This idea looked at the number of wheels growing in multiples of 2.
y-m-04-08.s.s1.o.b: Yes. 7 bicycles make 14 and 8 make 16, so you can fit it in between
y-m-04-08.s.s1.r.b: This idea missed that the number of vehicles must be a number you count, like 1, 2. Think about whether there is a number of vehicles between 7 and 8.
y-m-04-08.s.s1.o.c: You can't tell. Because you don't know how many bicycles there are
y-m-04-08.s.s1.r.c: This idea stopped at not knowing the number of vehicles. You can put down each possible number of vehicles one at a time and think about the number of wheels.
y-m-04-08.s.s1.explain: The number of bicycle wheels grows by 2s, like 2, 4, 6..., so 15 does not come up. So tricycles must be there too.
y-m-04-08.s.s2.prompt: Find 2 cases where there are a bicycles and b tricycles, both at least 1, and there are 15 wheels in all.
y-m-04-08.s.s2.hint.0: Put 1 tricycle and check whether the remaining number of wheels fits as bicycle wheels.
y-m-04-08.s.s2.hint.1: Do the same thing while changing the tricycles to 2, 3, and 4.
y-m-04-08.s.s2.ok.c1: There is at least 1 of each kind.
y-m-04-08.s.s2.fail.c1: The numbers of bicycles and tricycles must each be at least 1.
y-m-04-08.s.s2.fail.c2: The sum of the wheels is not 15. Count 2 for each bicycle and 3 for each tricycle.
y-m-04-08.s.s2.explain: They are 6 bicycles and 1 tricycle (12+3=15), and 3 bicycles and 3 tricycles (6+9=15). It is possible only when there are 1 or 3 tricycles.
y-m-04-08.s.s3.prompt: You also found out that there are 6 vehicles in all, bicycles and tricycles together. Of the two cases you just found, which one remains?
y-m-04-08.s.s3.hint.0: Add the number of bicycles and the number of tricycles in each of the two cases.
y-m-04-08.s.s3.hint.1: Compare whether the sum matches the new condition.
y-m-04-08.s.s3.r.a: This idea did not check whether the sum is 6. Count how many vehicles 6 and 1 make together.
y-m-04-08.s.s3.r.b: This idea saw that the new condition changes nothing. Check the sum of the numbers of vehicles in the two cases.
y-m-04-08.s.s3.r.c: This idea picked the case where the sum of the numbers of vehicles is 6.
y-m-04-08.s.s3.r.d: This idea did not check how the sums of the numbers of vehicles in the two cases differ from 6.
y-m-04-08.s.s3.explain: 6+1=7 vehicles and 3+3=6 vehicles, so the only case where the sum is 6 is 3 bicycles and 3 tricycles. The new condition narrowed the possible cases down to one.

y-m-04-09.title: How many patterns have 25 as the fifth number?
y-m-04-09.topic: Making a number arrangement that grows by the same amount
y-m-04-09.goal: Understand that in a number arrangement that 'grows by the same amount', if the first number and the amount it grows by are changed, there are several patterns that reach the same end, and make and explain your own pattern.
y-m-04-09.material: Lay out 5 numbers and make a pattern. Start from the first number and make it grow by the same amount each time. For example, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 grows by 2. This time you want the fifth number to be exactly 25. The first number and the amount it grows by are both countable numbers that are 1 or more.
y-m-04-09.thinking.0: Knowing that there can be several patterns
y-m-04-09.thinking.1: Making a pattern that fits the condition
y-m-04-09.thinking.2: Explaining your own pattern in words
y-m-04-09.prereq.0: Reading a number arrangement that grows by a constant amount (Grade 2 level)
y-m-04-09.s.s1.prompt: How many patterns can you make in which the fifth number is 25? (The first number and the amount it grows by have not been decided yet.)
y-m-04-09.s.s1.hint.0: When the first number is set as 5, test by how much it must grow to reach 25.
y-m-04-09.s.s1.hint.1: Change the first number to another number and do the same thing.
y-m-04-09.s.s1.o.a: There is only one. There is none except 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 growing by 5
y-m-04-09.s.s1.r.a: This idea stopped at the first one that came to mind. Change the first number or the amount it grows by and test whether you can reach 25.
y-m-04-09.s.s1.o.b: There are several. Even if you change the first number, you can reach 25
y-m-04-09.s.s1.r.b: This idea saw that you can change the first number and the amount it grows by.
y-m-04-09.s.s1.o.c: There are none. If you don't know the first number, you can't make a pattern
y-m-04-09.s.s1.r.c: This idea missed that you can decide for yourself what has not been decided.
y-m-04-09.s.s1.explain: You have to decide the first number and the amount it grows by, but there are several combinations. For example, patterns that start from 1 and grow by 6, start from 5 and grow by 5, and start from 21 and grow by 1 all reach 25.
y-m-04-09.s.s2.prompt: Make 4 patterns in which the fifth number is 25. Call the first number a and the amount it grows by d. Both are countable numbers that are 1 or more.
y-m-04-09.s.s2.hint.0: Decide the amount it grows by first and count how many times it grows to the last box.
y-m-04-09.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether the number that comes out is a countable number that is 1 or more.
y-m-04-09.s.s2.ok.c1: The first number and the amount it grows by are countable numbers that are 1 or more.
y-m-04-09.s.s2.fail.c1: The first number and the amount it grows by must both be countable numbers that are 1 or more.
y-m-04-09.s.s2.ok.c2: It grows 4 times, and the fifth number becomes 25.
y-m-04-09.s.s2.fail.c2: The fifth number is not 25. Add the amount it grows by four times to the first number.
y-m-04-09.s.s2.explain: The (first number, amount it grows by) pairs are (1, 6), (5, 5), (9, 4), (13, 3), (17, 2), and (21, 1). You can write 4 of these.
y-m-04-09.s.s2.because.prompt: Choose one of the patterns you made, write all five numbers, and explain in one sentence how it grows.
y-m-04-09.s.s2.because.hint.0: Start from the first number and write five numbers adding the amount it grows by one box at a time.
y-m-04-09.s.s2.because.hint.1: Check that the last number is 25 and say the amount it grows by.
y-m-04-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Are all five numbers there, and is the last one 25?
y-m-04-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you check that the differences between neighboring numbers are all the same?
y-m-04-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you say the amount it grows by clearly?
y-m-04-09.s.s2.because.model.1: It is a pattern 9, 13, 17, 21, 25 that grows by 4.
y-m-04-09.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: Shows both the start and the amount it grows by.
y-m-04-09.s.s3.explain: Line 2 grows by 5, but the fifth number is 23. Line 5 grows by 4, 4, 10, and 5, so it is not a pattern that grows by the same amount. Lines 1, 3, and 4 fit the condition.

y-m-04-10.title: From where is the skip counting wrong?
y-m-04-10.topic: Finding the mistake in a skip counting pattern
y-m-04-10.goal: Find the first mistake in numbers continued by following a pattern, understand why all the numbers after it are affected, find the correct numbers, and say a way to check.
y-m-04-10.material: Jiho started from 3 and skip counted by 4s. He wrote 'the number after this number' once on each line.
y-m-04-10.thinking.0: Finding an error by the difference of neighboring numbers
y-m-04-10.thinking.1: Judging the effect of an error on the numbers after it
y-m-04-10.prereq.0: Comparing neighboring numbers in a number arrangement (Grade 2 level)
y-m-04-10.s.s1.prompt: Pick the first wrong line among the lines Jiho wrote.
y-m-04-10.s.s1.hint.0: In each line, compare the number before and the number after.
y-m-04-10.s.s1.hint.1: Look for the line that continues differently from the first pattern.
y-m-04-10.s.s1.explain: It is line 4. 15 plus 4 is 19, but he wrote 20. Lines 1 to 3 are right. Lines 5 and 6 are right in that they 'added 4 to the number before', but line 4 is wrong, so the numbers that follow are different.
y-m-04-10.s.s2.prompt: Is the 28 that Jiho wrote at the end a number counted by skipping 4s from 3?
y-m-04-10.s.s2.hint.0: Write the correct number after 15 and compare it with 20.
y-m-04-10.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether the numbers after that also differ from the correct numbers by the same amount.
y-m-04-10.s.s2.o.a: Yes. Lines 5 and 6 added 4 to the number before, so 28 is right too
y-m-04-10.s.s2.r.a: This idea saw only that lines 5 and 6 kept the pattern. Check whether the 20 in line 4 carries on from the start.
y-m-04-10.s.s2.o.b: No. The mistake in line 4 carried over to the later numbers too
y-m-04-10.s.s2.r.b: This idea saw that a wrong place affects all the numbers after it.
y-m-04-10.s.s2.o.c: You can't tell. You have to redo lines 5 and 6 yourself to know
y-m-04-10.s.s2.r.c: This idea did not look at whether you can judge from the effect of the wrong place without redoing it.
y-m-04-10.s.s2.explain: The correct numbers are 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, and 27. Jiho's 20, 24, and 28 are all 1 greater than the correct numbers. After a wrong line, even if you continue by the pattern, the first mistake stays.
y-m-04-10.s.s3.prompt: Write, as words to say to Jiho, what he could check to find his mistake quickly.
y-m-04-10.s.s3.hint.0: Pick two neighboring numbers in Jiho's lines and write how you compared them.
y-m-04-10.s.s3.hint.1: Think of a way to show where the wrong place first appears.
y-m-04-10.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write what is compared with what?
y-m-04-10.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Are they words Jiho can follow?
y-m-04-10.s.s3.model.0: Compare one by one whether the numbers always grow by 4 between each pair. 15 and 20 differ by 5, so it is wrong.
y-m-04-10.s.s3.model.1: Subtract the two numbers next to each other and look for the place where the difference is not 4.
y-m-04-10.s.s3.modelNote.1: Said it as the checking action 'try subtracting'.

y-m-04-11.title: How far is the pattern of the 9 times table right?
y-m-04-11.topic: The tens and ones digit pattern of the 9 times table
y-m-04-11.goal: Test with more examples how far a pattern found from a few examples holds, find where the pattern breaks, and state it with a condition, 'it is right up to here'.
y-m-04-11.material: Eunwoo found a pattern while memorizing the 9 times table. 'In the 9 times table, each time the product grows by one step, the tens digit goes up by 1 and the ones digit goes down by 1.' (for example, 9, 18, 27...) If a product is a one-digit number, treat the tens digit as 0. Let's think by extending the multiplication table from 9×1 to 9×11.
y-m-04-11.thinking.0: Fixing how sure you are with new information
y-m-04-11.thinking.1: Finding the range in which a pattern holds
y-m-04-11.prereq.1: Knowing the tens digit and ones digit of a two-digit number (Grade 2 level)
y-m-04-11.s.s1.prompt: Think through Eunwoo's words by looking at information one piece at a time.
y-m-04-11.s.s1.hint.0: Write each product split into its tens digit and ones digit.
y-m-04-11.s.s1.hint.1: Compare how the tens digit and the ones digit each change between neighboring products.
y-m-04-11.s.s1.st.0.ask: What do you think about Eunwoo's words now?
y-m-04-11.s.s1.st.0.after: In 9, 18, 27, 36, and 45, the tens digit goes 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, growing by 1, and the ones digit goes 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, shrinking by 1. But we only looked at five.
y-m-04-11.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It is right for these five
y-m-04-11.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This idea checked whether it fits the data you can see.
y-m-04-11.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It's wrong. The ones digit getting smaller is a coincidence
y-m-04-11.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This idea denied it without checking the data. Split 9, 18, 27, 36, and 45 into the tens digit and the ones digit.
y-m-04-11.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It is always right in the whole 9 times table
y-m-04-11.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This idea decided the whole from five. There are products not yet looked at.
y-m-04-11.s.s1.st.1.info: Continuing, 9×6=54, 9×7=63, 9×8=72, and 9×9=81. In all of them, as Eunwoo said, the tens digit grows by 1 and the ones digit shrinks by 1.
y-m-04-11.s.s1.st.1.ask: How much can you trust Eunwoo's words now?
y-m-04-11.s.s1.st.1.after: Up to 9×9 the pattern is right. Whether it is right after that has not been checked yet, so both adding a condition and putting off checking are reasonable.
y-m-04-11.s.s1.st.1.o.a: You can say it is right in the multiplication table up to 9×9
y-m-04-11.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This idea added the condition that it is right within the range of the data seen.
y-m-04-11.s.s1.st.1.o.b: I only looked up to 9×9, so I don't know yet how it is after that
y-m-04-11.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This idea put off judging the range not looked at.
y-m-04-11.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Now I am sure it is surely right at 9×10 and 9×11 too
y-m-04-11.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This idea made a leap to products outside the range seen. Pick a product you want to check once more.
y-m-04-11.s.s1.st.2.info: 9×10=90. The tens digit grows by 1 from 8 to 9, and the ones digit shrinks by 1 from 1 to 0. 9×11=99. The tens digit stays 9 and the ones digit grows to 9.
y-m-04-11.s.s1.st.2.ask: Now how should Eunwoo's words be fixed?
y-m-04-11.s.s1.st.2.after: From 9×1 to 9×10=90 the pattern is right, and it breaks at 9×11=99. So you need to add the condition, 'a pattern that is right in the 9 times table up to 9×10'.
y-m-04-11.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It is always right in the whole 9 times table
y-m-04-11.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This idea did not take into account the newly seen 9×11=99.
y-m-04-11.s.s1.st.2.o.b: It was a wrong statement from the start
y-m-04-11.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This idea missed the fact that the pattern continued up to 9×10.
y-m-04-11.s.s1.st.2.o.c: It is right up to 9×10 and not right from 9×11
y-m-04-11.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This idea separated the range that is right and the place where it breaks.
y-m-04-11.s.s1.reflect: At first, you said it was right from five pieces of data, but you could have added a condition or put off judging. Only after seeing 9×11=99 did you learn how far the pattern is right. Say what information changed your sureness.
y-m-04-11.s.s2.prompt: Tell Eunwoo the range of multiplications where his words are right, and one multiplication where they are not right, writing it as a specific multiplication sentence or number.
y-m-04-11.s.s2.hint.0: Calculate in order the products after 9×9 and check whether the pattern is right.
y-m-04-11.s.s2.hint.1: Find the product where the pattern first stops being right and write that product.
y-m-04-11.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you show how far it is right, with a number or multiplication sentence?
y-m-04-11.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you give one breaking product and say why it breaks?
y-m-04-11.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you avoid saying Eunwoo's words are completely wrong or completely right?
y-m-04-11.s.s2.model.0: It is right up to 9×10=90, but in 9×11=99 the tens digit stays at 9, so the pattern breaks.
y-m-04-11.s.s2.model.1: It is fine up to 9×9=81. In 9×11=99 the ones digit actually grows, so it does not fit Eunwoo's words.
y-m-04-11.s.s2.modelNote.1: Said the range that is right as up to 9×9 and gave one breaking product.

y-m-04-12.title: Do blocks grow by the same amount at each step?
y-m-04-12.topic: How the number of blocks grows in a staircase shape
y-m-04-12.goal: Throw away a pattern built from two points when it does not fit a third piece of data, and find and explain the pattern of how the number grows from the shape being made.
y-m-04-12.thinking.0: Checking a pattern built from little data
y-m-04-12.thinking.2: Finding the reason for a pattern from the shape
y-m-04-12.prereq.1: Looking at the amount that grows in a number arrangement (Grade 2 level)
y-m-04-12.s.s1.prompt: How many blocks are needed in all for a 4-step staircase?
y-m-04-12.s.s1.r.a: This idea continued counting by looking only at the difference of the first two. Check whether it matches the 6 blocks of 3 steps.
y-m-04-12.s.s1.r.b: This idea saw it as growing by 3 from the 6 of 3 steps. Check the number of blocks in the new bottom row.
y-m-04-12.s.s1.r.c: This idea used the number of blocks in the newly made bottom row.
y-m-04-12.s.s1.r.d: This idea multiplied by 3 for each step. Check with the shape.
y-m-04-12.s.s1.explain: Adding the 4 blocks of the new bottom row of 4 steps to the 6 for up to 3 steps makes 10. From 1 step to 2 steps it grows by 2, from 2 to 3 steps by 3, and from 3 to 4 steps by 4.
y-m-04-12.s.s2.prompt: Dohyeon explained to Harin. Pick the wrong line.
y-m-04-12.s.s2.hint.0: Write in order the numbers added in lines 1 and 2.
y-m-04-12.s.s2.line.0: 1 step is 1 block and 2 steps is 1+2=3 blocks.
y-m-04-12.s.s2.line.1: 3 steps is 3+3=6 blocks and 4 steps is 6+4=10 blocks.
y-m-04-12.s.s2.line.2: So each time a step is added, the blocks always grow by 2.
y-m-04-12.s.s2.explain: Line 3 is wrong. The number of blocks added changes: 2, 3, 4, 5. Lines 1, 2, and 4 are right because they explain by adding the number of blocks in the new bottom row.
y-m-04-12.s.s3.prompt: Tell Harin why 4 steps is not 8, using the shape or numbers.
y-m-04-12.s.s3.hint.0: Write the number you counted for the blocks newly placed when going from 3 steps to 4 steps.
y-m-04-12.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether the growing by 2 that Harin said is right for going from 2 steps to 3 steps too.
y-m-04-12.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say the number of blocks for 4 steps as a specific number?
y-m-04-12.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you use the new bottom row or the number that grows as your reason?
y-m-04-12.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you avoid saying only that Harin's words are simply wrong?
y-m-04-12.s.s3.model.0: For 4 steps, adding the 4 blocks of the bottom row to the 6 of 3 steps makes 10. The amount it grows is different each time, like 2, 3, 4.
y-m-04-12.s.s3.model.1: If you make the bottom row 4 in a picture and count, there are 10 in all. It doesn't grow by 2 each time.
y-m-04-12.s.s3.modelNote.1: Convinced by the method of drawing a picture and counting.
